final_note: You worked through Monoclonal Antibodies (biology only) — 7 specification statements.

concepts.def: An antibody produced from a single clone of cells. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.

The cell made when mouse lymphocytes, which have been stimulated to make a particular antibody, are combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody.

concepts.term: Cloning and purification of the antibody
concepts.def: Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody. A large amount of the antibody can then be collected and purified.

concepts.term: Monoclonal antibodies in diagnosis and research
concepts.def: Uses that depend on the antibody binding to one specific antigen: for diagnosis, such as in pregnancy tests; in laboratories to measure the levels of hormones and other chemicals in blood, or to detect pathogens; and in research to locate or identify specific molecules in a cell or tissue by binding to them with a fluorescent dye.

For cancer, the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing. It delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

mcqs.q: Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody. They are then combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. What does the tumour cell allow the hybridoma cell to do?
options: Make the antibody that is later collected.
Make a different antibody as it divides.
Divide to produce many identical cells.
Kill the cells the antibody binds to.
mcqs.explain: Correct. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody, and single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody.

mcqs.q: A monoclonal antibody is collected from a clone of hybridoma cells and used to measure the level of one hormone in blood. Why does it bind only to that hormone?
options: It is made by a mixture of many different cells.
It is specific to one binding site on one antigen.
It is made by one particular kind of tumour cell.
It is able to bind any antigen in the sample.
mcqs.explain: Correct. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical in the body.

mcqs.q: A patient with cancer is given a monoclonal antibody that has been bound to a toxic drug. The antibody binds to an antigen found on the patient's cancer cells. How does this treatment work?
options: It carries the toxic drug to every body cell.
It stops the toxic drug causing side effects.
It destroys the cancer cells as it binds to them.
It delivers the toxic drug to the cancer cells.
mcqs.explain: Correct. For cancer the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a toxic drug, and it delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

mcqs.q: Which statement about monoclonal antibodies is correct?
options: They create more side effects than expected.
They bind to several different protein antigens.
They create fewer side effects than expected.
They kill cancer cells with no substance bound.
mcqs.explain: Correct. Monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected, and they are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed.
